title: Marble Into Breath
tagline: He sculpted the soul of Baroque Rome into stone and light.

scenes.text: Rome, 1620s. The 25-year-old Bernini completes Apollo and Daphne — marble that moves, that breathes, where a god's fingers reach and a woman transforms into laurel. Rome is astonished.
Pope Urban VIII becomes his patron. Bernini is handed the keys to the Eternal City itself — he will shape it for fifty years.

challenge.fact: Apollo and Daphne (1622–1625) shows the moment Daphne transforms into a laurel tree to escape Apollo — her fingers becoming branches, bark creeping up her legs. Bernini carved this in marble when he was in his mid-twenties. Viewers reported that the finished work looked impossible, as if he had found a way to capture a single instant of motion in stone.
challenge.instruction: Cardinal Scipione Borghese has filled his villa with the young Bernini's marbles. Place each work in the room that shows it best, with Apollo and Daphne where it can astonish.

scenes.text: He designs the baldachin above St. Peter's tomb — 30 meters of twisted bronze columns pulling the eye upward into Michelangelo's dome. Theater and architecture as one.

challenge.instruction: Above St Peter's tomb the bronze baldachin rises, crawling with Urban VIII's Barberini bees, laurel and suns. Match the emblems as Bernini's foundry casts and gilds them.
challenge.fact: Bernini's baldachin (1624–1634) rises about 29 m over the tomb of St Peter on four twisted bronze columns modelled on the ancient columns of Old St Peter's. Urban VIII had bronze stripped from the Pantheon's portico, much of it for cannon at Castel Sant'Angelo, prompting Romans to quip: 'What the barbarians did not do, the Barberini did.'

scenes.text: His Ecstasy of Saint Teresa scandalizes and mesmerizes — a nun in rapture, angels with golden arrows, light streaming through hidden windows. It is a complete theatrical experience.

challenge.instruction: Bernini wants St Teresa to glow as if lit from heaven, by a source no worshipper can see. Steer the daylight from his hidden window down onto the saint and the angel.
challenge.fact: The Cornaro Chapel in Santa Maria della Vittoria (1647–1652) was commissioned by Cardinal Federico Cornaro. A window concealed above the altar pours daylight down gilded bronze rays onto Teresa and the angel, while marble members of the Cornaro family watch from theatre boxes on the side walls.

scenes.text: The great colonnade of St. Peter's Square: two arms of columns wrapping the faithful in an embrace. Bernini says they represent the Church reaching out to the world.

challenge.instruction: Bernini's colonnade wraps St Peter's Square in four rows of columns. Leap through every bay of the square once, touching the numbered marks in order, as a pilgrim crossing the motherly arms of the Church.
challenge.fact: Bernini designed St. Peter's Square's twin colonnades to open at their ends, creating a welcoming gesture toward the city. He described them as 'the motherly arms of the Church' reaching out to embrace the faithful — Catholics to confirm their faith, heretics to reunite with the Church, and unbelievers to discover the light. The design is both engineering and theology.

params.title: The Colonnade of St Peter’s
params.intro: Bernini’s colonnade (1656–1667) frames St Peter’s Square. Leap through every bay of the square once, landing on the numbered marks in order — 1, then 2, then 3. A numbered mark cannot be entered early.
params.fact: Bernini built the colonnade of St Peter’s Square for Alexander VII between 1656 and 1667: 284 columns in four rows, topped by 140 statues of saints.

scenes.text: Bernini outlives his rivals and his patrons. He works into his 80s and dies in 1680 — the man who made Rome Baroque, who turned marble into belief.

challenge.instruction: In his last winter a great comet hangs over Rome. Plot its path through the astronomers' sightings, the last wonder of the sky Bernini will see.
challenge.fact: Bernini died in Rome on 28 November 1680, aged 81, a fortnight after Gottfried Kirch first saw the Great Comet. He had served popes from Paul V to Innocent XI, and was buried in Santa Maria Maggiore beneath a plain slab in the floor.

challenge.instruction: In his late sixties Bernini turns the old bridge to Castel Sant'Angelo into a Way of the Cross lined with angels. Lead the pilgrims over every bridge once and home to St Peter's.
challenge.fact: In 1667 Clement IX commissioned ten angels for the Ponte Sant'Angelo, each holding an instrument of the Passion. Bernini designed them all and carved two himself — the angels with the Crown of Thorns and the Superscription — which the pope kept from the weather; they are now in Sant'Andrea delle Fratte.

scenes.speaker: Gian Lorenzo Bernini
scenes.text: Two face-down cards: one at St Petersburg, one at London. We cannot see who they are until we attack, and an attack reveals every card at the location. The Art Critique already runs at St Petersburg; you hold a card to start one at London.

challenge.instruction: Fight lesson 5 · Face Down. Win two attacks: fight at St Petersburg where the Art Critique is running, then carry the fight to London by starting your own event there.
challenge.fact: A card on the board can be public (face up) or private (face down). A private card hides its identity and stats from rivals until an attack reveals every card at that location. Your own cards deploy face down; Go Public when being seen helps you.
